paragraphs: “Ask General Xie to wait another three days.”

Fu Jian spoke calmly. The Jin envoy stared at him. Fu Pi’s hand paused upon his sword hilt. No one in the imperial tent dared speak. Outside, drops of rain slipped from the leather awning and struck the bronze basin set beneath it.
“And after three days?” the envoy asked.
“I shall give him an answer.”
“If the King of Qin is afraid to fight—”
“Tell Xie Xuan,” Fu Jian interrupted, “that I am not afraid to face him. But I will not let these few yards of river decide who shall live and die among all the people under heaven.”

The Jin envoy bowed and withdrew. That night no order to retreat came from the central army. Meals were served and patrols made as usual. Only the quartermasters and scouts of the several commands were summoned to the lamps, arriving one party after another with marching records stained by silt. At first the generals could not understand what the emperor intended. By dawn of the next day, officers had already been sent to the roads behind the army to register horses at the intersections, wagon convoys, and units awaiting reassignment separately.

The road inspectors divided into three parties. One took wooden rulers to measure the deck of the old bridge across the Ru River. Another counted the raised slopes where troops could camp above the marshes. The third followed the village lanes requisitioned for the march to see how many ox carts might still use them. Headquarters listed the camps that could move to the rear at once, then entered separately the cavalry detachments only just returned from escorting grain. Two clerks argued themselves red in the face over the whereabouts of a thousand-man unit. Only when its chief of staff appeared with a mud-streaked order transferring its posting were the missing soldiers added to the roll.
Fu Pi could bear it no longer. He entered the tent and demanded, “If Your Majesty has no intention of fighting, why bring the army all this way?”
Fu Jian studied his son for a long time before replying. “That is what I am asking myself.”
“The Jin number no more than a few tens of thousands. There will never be another chance like this.”
“Is your chance the few banners you have seen, or the grain you can guarantee will reach the far bank?”
Fu Pi’s face burned. “Let your son lead the vanguard across. The rest of the army need not follow.”
“If you win, how will you hold the ground? If you lose, who will come for you?”
“Your son is not afraid to die.”
“I am.”
Fu Pi raised his head. The word *afraid* was one his father had never used lightly between them.
“I am afraid you will die, and that many more will die with you. I brought you here to learn how to command men, not to make good the regrets I have carried.”

Even Fu Jian was taken aback by his own words. Many years earlier, when Wang Meng lay ill, he had urged the emperor to leave the realm to those who came after him. At the time Fu Jian had thought the counsel merely an old man’s surrender at the end of life. Now the youth of those years wore a general’s seal. Looking at him, Fu Jian remembered how long Wang Meng had gazed toward the young imperial princes beyond the hall when he spoke of leaving the realm to posterity.

On the morning of the third day, Xie Xuan ascended the watchtower on the southern bank. He saw Qin banners being shifted along the roads to the rear and knew the enemy had not withdrawn from its position as he had anticipated. He summoned his generals. Some urged launching the boats while the northern army still hesitated. Xie Xuan refused and asked only whether the flotilla could be gathered within half a day. Assured that it could, he ordered twice the usual number of scouts on the southern bank and prepared to receive the Qin answer.

The southern shore had not been idle overnight either. Local people reclaimed more than a dozen small craft lent to the army before the battle. Two boat-owning families, anxious that Qin might really withdraw, asked whether the army would still compensate them for the wooden oars it had requisitioned. A Beifu clerk circled the numbers of boats not yet returned, one by one. As Xie Xuan descended from the tower, he saw an old man holding fast to the register, asking only for the ancestral bronze bell from his boat. Xie Xuan ordered the storehouse opened to find it. Inside, what lay in the greatest heaps were broken oars not yet repaired.
A staff officer was puzzled. “We asked him to retreat. If he refuses, have we not lost our opportunity?”
“If he moves, we can see where he is weak,” Xie Xuan replied. “If he stays, we have learned something else.”
“What?”
“Not everyone in Qin necessarily wishes to fight this battle.”

Xie Xuan took no pride in the remark. He still remembered the broken oar in the boatyard, and the archer who had lain burning with fever the previous night. Even should the enemy expose a weakness, he did not wish to gamble his soldiers' lives against a trap he had not properly examined.

On the northern bank, Fu Rong had inspected the lines of withdrawal twice. The first inspection covered the main roads alone; for the second he sent men to ford crossings, village paths, and bridges as well. Someone suggested moving the entire rear camp to Runan. Murong Chui objected firmly. “Move the whole army in one day, and we shall block our own escape.”

He required a unit capable of turning and forming ranks every few li, with grain wagons moving first, the wounded and sick in the middle, and cavalry screening the rear. Headquarters would verify the numbers camp by camp, and the Secretariat and imperial headquarters would seal the records separately. The three seals were no longer an old court procedure for contending over power. Here they determined which unit could move first and which must remain until nightfall.

At the third check of the orders, a convoy of grain wagons had already harnessed its oxen under an oral instruction from the previous day. But the sequence of bridges in the military headquarters schedule differed by two hours from the itinerary issued by the central secretariat, and the wagons were trapped outside the tent. Fu Rong spread the post-road map across a cart shaft himself and told the convoy chief to lead the beasts onto a side track to rest. A clerk carried away the departure slip signed by Fu Jian, added the order in which the bridges were to be crossed, and returned it to the offices for verification. The drivers cursed for a while, then discovered that the delay had given several damaged wagons time for their axles to be repaired.

Yao Chang requested leave to escort the officials responsible for ritual back north. He held no fighting command, he said, and should not remain at the front for long. Fu Jian permitted him to withdraw with the central camp, but ordered his escort chosen by military headquarters; he was not to summon former followers on his own authority. Yao Chang received the order with every show of obedience. Outside the tent, however, he glanced toward the water in the south. The Fei ran between the reed flowers, carrying away not so much as the echo of a horn.

In the afternoon Fu Jian summoned Zhu Xu again. He asked nothing of military secrets, only about the people who had once lived in Xiangyang. Some remained in the city, Zhu Xu told him. Some had gone south supporting their elders and carrying their children. Others wished only to return and tend their ancestors' graves. Fu Jian fell silent. The hundred and fifty thousand armored men he had seen on the parade ground at Luoyang had troubled him less than these few ordinary sentences.
“If there is no battle today, will you return to Jin?” Fu Jian asked.
Zhu Xu looked at him. “Will Your Majesty let me go?”
“If I release you, will you leave?”
“I will.”
“And once home, will you fight against me again?”
“If my country requires it, I will.”
Fu Jian gave a wry smile. “You really will not say a single thing to please me.”
“If I knew how, perhaps Xiangyang would not have held out for as long as it did.”

Fu Jian ordered Zhu Xu to remain for the present in the central camp. Once the two sides had settled arrangements for the withdrawal, they could discuss whether he would be free to go. Zhu Xu bowed, but offered no further thanks. Whether or not the battle took place, he knew he could not lightly untie the knot left by those who had died at Xiangyang.

That evening Fu Rong brought Fu Jian the verified records of the roads to the rear. The hundred and fifty thousand fighting men who had advanced south could retire northward in stages within ten days, but the laborers and grain wagons of all the contingents would need longer to cross the bridges. If the vanguard fell back at once to lure the Jin across, its orders would be difficult to convey to the last ranks. One false report of defeat might cause the camps to trample one another. Hold the northern bank and both sides would consume grain, while Qin could not afford to stay indefinitely. Force the crossing and the Jin could defend the waterline, while Qin’s supplies could not be delivered in an unbroken flow. There were three roads on paper; not one offered the emperor easy satisfaction.

When Fu Jian had finished reading, he ordered an old letter brought to him, written by Wang Meng before his death. The paper had yellowed, and its edges had grown soft from his touch. He did not read it aloud. He placed it beside the campaign map. It was a reminder left him by a dead man, and a pledge he himself had spoken, whose ten years had not yet run their course.
Fu Pi still stood at the side of the tent, stubbornness in his eyes. Murong Chui remained silent a long while. Fu Rong waited for an order.

“When I first heard Xie Xuan’s challenge,” Fu Jian said at last, “I thought he was delivering himself into my hands. But when I came to the river, I found our army already tethered by its roads and grain. The enemy stands before us. Victory may still be possible. Yet if we lose the hearts of our people today, taking a few cities will not win them back.”
He ordered a scribe to grind the ink.

“Write back to Xie Xuan. The two armies will hold their respective banks. The Qin army will withdraw north in stages. If the Jin do not pursue, we will advance no farther south. If they attack during our withdrawal, each camp will defend itself under its standing orders.”
Fu Pi dropped abruptly to his knees. “Father, I beg you to reconsider!”
Fu Jian looked at him but did not tell him to rise.
“What have you seen here?”
“The Jin army.”
“What else?”
Fu Pi bit his lip, and finally answered, “Our grain wagons as well.”
Fu Jian nodded. “When you command an army one day, do not forget the people who follow behind it.”

By the time the letter went out, dusk had fallen. The river wind carried the clean, bitter scent of reeds across the tents. On the southern bank Xie Xuan received the reply and examined the seals before reading its words. Xie Shi asked whether the Qin would really leave. Xie Xuan said, “We shall see tomorrow.”
“And if they do?”
“Hold Huainan.”
“If they do not?”
“Hold Huainan all the same.”

Xie Xuan passed the letter around to his officers and ordered the boat patrols to continue through the night as usual. He was in no hurry to proclaim victory. To spare the people of Jin a vast calamity of war was no less a thing than cutting down a hundred thousand men on the battlefield.

The messengers carrying the withdrawal order reached the rear camps first. One new unit number did not match an entry in the old regimental rolls. The veteran camp commander pointed at his banner and said he had only that morning been ordered to guard the grain road; now he was to withdraw first. Had something happened to the imperial camp? Before his eyes the central headquarters officer broke open three separate seals, read the full order for a staged withdrawal, and instructed him to send men along the route repeating it aloud. Only after nightfall did each unit nail the notice to its grain wagons. The first animals due to depart remained tethered; not one was allowed to move ahead on its own.

Five days later, the rear of the Qin army began to leave the river in stages. The draft animals and grain wagons went first, then the wounded, the sick, and the laborers. Infantry stood with shields along the roads, while cavalry watched the northwestern tracks. The column of more than a hundred thousand moved with painful slowness. Some complained that the emperor had marched them here for nothing; others rejoiced that they would no longer have to cross that river in unending rain. The elderly Di soldier put on the boots he had finished sewing and showed his stitches to a comrade, not knowing whether there would be another campaign after this one.

At the bridgehead on the northern bank, a wagon of wounded soldiers was long delayed. The left wheel of the medical cart had sunk into a hole left by the previous night’s flood. The grain convoy ahead had already moved away, and the infantry behind could not halt for long. Two young horsemen, assigned to escort the last cavalry unit, dismounted and together lifted the cart shaft. The wounded men urged them to hurry for fear of missing the roll call in their camp. Their commanding officer wrote down the two men’s names in the little bridge-crossing register. He promised no reward; he told them only to rejoin their unit before its banner disappeared.

Fu Jian walked down to the water’s edge last. He neither boarded a boat nor ordered a bridge built. Deep among the reeds on the opposite shore, the Jin sentries changed watch; someone in the distance lowered a flag. Soldiers of the two states watched one another across the water for a long time, without shouting insults or cheering.
Fu Rong came to ask the emperor to mount and return. Fu Jian nodded and looked south one final time.

He had once believed that crossing this river would bring all under heaven together. Now its waters still flowed east, and the Yangtze lay far away to the south. Wang Meng had been dead many years, but the ten years he had left behind were not yet over. Fu Jian could not claim to have abandoned his wish to unite the realm. For the first time, however, he was willing to acknowledge that an emperor’s desire might wait, while the dead could never be called back to life.
He turned his horse. The Qin banners pointed north in the wind, and the orders were relayed one after another down the line.

There was no great rout on the banks of the Fei River, no disaster that would shake the realm in the years to come. What remained were damp river flats, sentries who kept their watch on either shore, and the unanswered question that countless soldiers carried home: if neither side had won or lost, what had this long march been for?
Fu Jian had yet to answer that question himself.
